findings.headline: Void times for temporary accommodation are long enough that the council prioritises a dedicated repairs contract to reduce them
findings.detail: The council expects the new contract will reduce void times (periods when units sit empty). If the contract is not successfully awarded, void times would worsen and create additional strain on the existing HRA contractor.
findings.matters: Extended voids directly reduce rental income from temporary accommodation and undermine the efficiency of the council's emergency housing provision, affecting financial sustainability of the HRA.
findings.figures: None provided in this document.
findings.quote: Possible impacts if the contract is not successfully awarded, impacting void times and further strain to the current HRA contract.

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance work for council housing is currently outside the scope of the existing HRA contract, creating performance risk
findings.detail: Medway relies on HRA contractors to undertake repairs and maintenance for temporary accommodation and other council-owned properties that fall outside their formal contract scope. The council has identified that this arrangement risks impacting the contractors' performance against their contractual obligations and threatening HRA operational performance.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced for financial purposes; disruption to contractor performance directly threatens the council's ability to maintain service delivery, asset management, and rental income across its housing stock.
findings.figures: None provided in this document.
findings.quote: This is outside of current contract scope and risks impacting performance of the contractual obligations and thus performance of the HRA.

findings.headline: Council is relying on predominantly short-term borrowing due to market volatility, facing £150m refinancing need in the year ahead
findings.detail: The council's borrowing strategy has been primarily short-term due to market volatility and elevated interest rates. While officers acknowledge a balanced short and long-term portfolio would be preferable, they are reviewing options with treasury advisors. The council has £150m of loans maturing during the year that will need refinancing, some at rates higher than those locked in previously.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on short-term borrowing and refinancing of £150m during elevated rates creates significant refinancing risk and makes the council vulnerable to further rate rises or market disruption.
findings.figures: £215.5m short-term borrowing (up from £184.5m at 31 March); £150m loans maturing; short-term borrowing rate 4.33%; 5-year PWLB rate 5.07%
findings.quote: The Authority's borrowing decisions have been manly been predicated the need to borrow short term due to the volitility in the markets and heightened interest rates in the recent past.

findings.headline: Strategic property fund investments are generating capital losses and delivering only 9.5% of budgeted income
findings.detail: The £14.3m invested in externally managed pooled property funds generated £90k unrealised capital loss in Q1 alone. Income received by 30 June was only £50k against a full-year budget of £526k. One fund (Patrizia Hanover) ceased trading and was taken over; 164 of 354 units held remain to be redeemed as the fund realises capital.
findings.matters: Underperforming investment income reduces reserves available to fund operations; capital losses erode the balance sheet at a time when financing costs are exceeding budget.
findings.figures: £90k unrealised capital loss in Q1; £50k income received vs £526k budgeted (9.5% of annual budget); £2.9m partial fund redemption; 164 units still pending redemption
findings.quote: Over the quarter, these funds generated an overall £90,000 of unrealised capital loss.

findings.headline: £40 million of LOBO loans have call dates within the next 12 months, creating active refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council holds £50.5m of LOBO loans where lenders can propose rate increases at set dates. £40m of this portfolio will have call dates within 12 months. As market rates have risen, the probability of call options being exercised is increased. If exercised, the council plans to repay using available cash or new borrowing, but this forces refinancing at potentially much higher rates.
findings.matters: LOBO call exercises would force immediate refinancing of £40m at potentially significantly higher rates during a period when the council is already stressed on financing costs.
findings.figures: £40m of £50.5m LOBO portfolio callable in next 12 months; current LOBO rate 4.33%; short-term borrowing rate 4.33%
findings.quote: The Authority has £40million LOBO loans with call dates within the next 12 months.

findings.headline: Council now expects to require Exceptional Financial Support in the current year, with debt reaching £800-900m by local government reorganisation
findings.detail: When questioned about impact on the successor North Kent authority, the Chief Operating Officer stated the council now expects EFS in the current year to be added to council debt. By the vesting day for reorganisation, debt is expected to be £800-900m, in addition to £200m held by Dartford and Gravesham councils. Government has only allocated £900k to support LGR costs despite the council needing much more.
findings.matters: EFS is a clear signal the council cannot meet its statutory duties from its own resources. Combined with local government reorganisation, this indicates financial stress and elevated refinancing risk for the successor authority.
findings.figures: Projected debt £800m-£900m; Dartford and Gravesham combined debt £200m; EFS now required; only £900k government funding for LGR against significant need
findings.quote: By vesting day, it was likely that the Council's debt would reach between £800m-£900m

findings.headline: Financing and interest costs are forecast to overspend by £4.2m, primarily because interest rates are higher than budgeted
findings.detail: The budget assumed rates would remain flat when set in February 2026, but rates have risen. Interest paid is forecast at £33.4m against a budget of £28.5m, an overspend of £4.9m. The Chief Operating Officer noted that with significant capital projects underway and £150m of loans maturing during the year, there is limited scope for improvement save mitigation within departments.
findings.matters: A council unable to forecast financing costs creates refinancing and budget risk, particularly with substantial maturing debt and higher-for-longer rate expectations.
findings.figures: £4.162m total financing overspend; Interest paid £33.387m vs budget £28.497m; £150m loans maturing in year
findings.quote: At the end of round one, there was a forecast £4.162m pressure on the financing and interest budget, primarily caused by higher than anticipated interest rates.

findings.headline: Key contractors underperformed during 2025/26, prompting shift toward increased direct labour and enhanced management
findings.detail: The HRA Governance Group identified and actively challenged performance issues with key contractors on repairs and maintenance. Response included enhanced contract management, regular review meetings, reduced subcontractor reliance, and actions to increase direct labour capacity within the council.
findings.matters: Service delivery problems with repairs contractors indicate operational challenges; strategic shift toward direct labour signals either contractor market capacity constraints or council dissatisfaction with external delivery capability.
findings.figures: No figures specified
findings.quote: Performance issues with key contractors were actively challenged, with enhanced contract management, regular review meetings, and actions to improve communication, reduce subcontractor reliance, and increase direct labour capacity.

findings.headline: £2.5 million capital programme underway at St Albans Close including full balcony replacement and fire safety upgrades
findings.detail: Major estate (St Albans Close, Gillingham) receiving comprehensive improvement programme: full balcony replacements, fire door upgrades, enhanced insulation, and communal area improvements. This addresses structural and fire safety compliance on one of the council's largest estates.
findings.matters: Capital spending on aging housing stock, particularly structural repairs and fire safety compliance, reflects asset condition and council investment in maintaining housing standards.
findings.figures: £2.5 million programme
findings.quote: £2.5 million programme of improvement works at St Albans Close in Gillingham, one of our largest estates. This programme includes full balcony replacements, fire door upgrades, enhanced insulation, and a range of improvements to communal areas.

findings.headline: Council conducting regulatory and financial due diligence on acquisition of a Registered Provider's housing portfolio
findings.detail: Due diligence has commenced on proposed transfer of a Registered Provider's housing portfolio into the HRA. Subject to approval, this would increase the council's housing stock, ensure existing tenants benefit from council management, and contribute to meeting future housing demand.
findings.matters: Portfolio transfer would expand the HRA's asset base and liabilities, committing council resources to manage additional properties and tenants; lenders assess council capacity to absorb such acquisitions.
findings.figures: Portfolio size not yet specified; still in due diligence phase
findings.quote: Regulatory and financial due diligence has commenced in relation to the proposed transfer of a Registered Provider's housing portfolio within the borough into the HRA.

findings.headline: Medway HRA holds RSH C2 regulator grading and is working through quarterly improvement plan toward C1
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing assigned C2 grading to the HRA's landlord services. The HRA Governance Group oversees quarterly review and scrutiny of a formal continuous improvement plan to progress toward C1 grading, with reporting to Cabinet and Council Management Team.
findings.matters: Regulatory grading by the Regulator of Social Housing reflects service quality and compliance in housing management; C2 indicates areas of concern that required formal improvement planning.
findings.figures: C2 current grading, C1 target
findings.quote: The Group continues to review, monitor and scrutinise the service's continuous improvement plan in response to the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) C2 grading.

findings.headline: Void numbers increased 23% with turnaround times severely above target
findings.detail: Void properties rose from 203 in 2024/25 to 250 in 2025/26. Ten-day voids averaged 78.4 days (7.8x the target), while twenty-day voids averaged 158.9 days (nearly 8x target). Mears' delays accounted for 127 of those 158 days on complex voids. Annual rent loss reimbursement claim was £31,998.77.
findings.matters: Rising void rate indicates asset turnover and management problems; extended turnaround times reduce rental income and suggest operational constraints; high voids may also signal broader housing demand or quality issues.
findings.figures: Voids: 250 in 2025/26 vs 203 in 2024/25 (+23.15%); ten-day turnaround 78.4 days vs 10-day target; twenty-day turnaround 158.9 days vs 20-day target; annual rent loss £31,998.77
findings.quote: 250 properties were void in 2025/26 compared to 203 in 2024/25 - 23.15% increase.

findings.headline: Roofing capital programme severely delayed across all property types
findings.detail: Pitched roofs to houses are only 23.2% complete, blocks 0% (pending S20 consultation), and flat roofs 50%. The council explicitly identifies roofing as the main delivery concern, attributed to late starts, access issues, and earlier commercial constraints. This represents a major slippage in the capital works schedule.
findings.matters: Weak capital delivery on a core maintenance category signals either budget pressures, contractor performance problems, or scope issues; significant slippage will require future spending acceleration or deferral of other works.
findings.figures: Pitched roofs to houses: 23.2% complete; Blocks: 0% complete (pending S20); Flat roofs: 50% complete
findings.quote: Roofing is the main delivery concern, with pitched roofs to houses at 23.2%, blocks at 0% (pending S20), and flat roofs at 50%, reflecting late starts, access issues, and earlier commercial constraints.

findings.headline: Fire Risk Assessment has 265 overdue actions with 60% delayed over 12 months
findings.detail: Of 1,129 total FRA actions, 265 remain open (23%). The critical issue is that 158 of these (60%) are overdue by more than 12 months, with the worst categories being FED (64 items over 12 months late), Compartmentation (57 over 12 months), and Tenant actions (52 over 6–12 months). A regulatory self-referral review found no material non-compliance requiring Regulator notification, but the backlog remains substantial.
findings.matters: A historic compliance backlog, even if currently below regulatory threshold, represents operational risk and asset safety concerns that lenders monitor as indicators of management capability.
findings.figures: 265 open actions; 158 (60%) overdue by 12+ months; FED 64 overdue 12+ months; Compartmentation 57 overdue 12+ months
findings.quote: All 265 open actions are overdue, with 158 (60%) overdue by more than 12 months, indicating a historic backlog.

findings.headline: Repairs service targets missed across urgent and routine work
findings.detail: Urgent repairs achieved 89.15% against 100% target, routine repairs 88.26% against 99% target, and appointment keeping 88.26% against 99.5% target in 2025-26. The council attributes this to capacity, scheduling, or access issues. A recruitment programme is in place but has not yet reversed the downward trend.
findings.matters: Service delivery failures indicate potential staffing or cost pressures; widespread appointment misses affect tenant satisfaction and could signal underlying operational problems that increase future maintenance costs.
findings.figures: Urgent repairs: 100% target, 89.15% actual; Routine repairs: 99% target, 88.26% actual; Appointments: 99.5% target, 88.26% actual
findings.quote: Urgent, routine repairs and appointment keeping are materially underperforming in 2025-26.

findings.headline: KPSN circuit consolidation proposes £100k capital investment to achieve ongoing cost avoidance through infrastructure reuse.
findings.detail: The programme requires £100,000 capital (split across 2026/27 and 2027/28) to consolidate data circuits, with a claim that it will 'reduce revenue costs to KPSN'. The mechanism is described as decommissioning redundant circuits and repurposing existing infrastructure (e.g., reconfiguring a traffic-signal circuit to also carry CCTV and IoT traffic). Benefits are stated as 'reduced ongoing costs through fewer circuit rentals and simplified support arrangements.'
findings.matters: If delivered, this represents efficient use of borrowing to fund operational cost avoidance. A finance director should track whether the promised savings on circuit rentals materialize; a lender might view this as evidence of operational discipline, but only if the savings are real.
findings.quote: Yes upfront cost to cover migration costs but will reduce revenue costs to KPSN Borrowing 100,000 100,000

findings.headline: A £580,000 Security Operations Centre investment claims to deliver revenue savings but depends on successful 5-year procurement agreement.
findings.detail: The SOC is allocated £580,000 in capital (split 2026/27 and 2027/28) with a claim that 'procuring 5 year agreement will see a savings to revenue costs.' The business case describes 24/7 monitoring and incident response capabilities, but the financial benefit relies on negotiating and delivering a 5-year service contract. If savings do not materialize, the council will have borrowed £580k for a discretionary service with no revenue offset.
findings.matters: A finance director must track whether these savings are delivered; shortfalls will create pressure on revenue budgets. A lender should verify that claimed savings are realistic before treating this investment as financially neutral.
findings.figures: £580,000 capital investment; claimed revenue savings from 5-year procurement agreement
findings.quote: Yes - procuring 5 year agreement will see a savings to revenue costs Borrowing 580,000 580,000

findings.headline: Multiple critical ICT systems are end-of-life and require immediate replacement to prevent operational failure.
findings.detail: The Brocade LAN switching infrastructure (in service since 2016) is 'now approaching or have reached end-of-life (EOL) status, with limited vendor support, no firmware updates, and increasing hardware failure risk.' Server infrastructure has reached 'end-of-support status' with 'critical firmware updates, security patches, and hardware replacements are no longer guaranteed.' Cisco routers and industrial switches are 'end-of-life and no longer supported by the manufacturer.' These are not optional upgrades but essential to maintain network reliability, security compliance (NCSC best practice), and service continuity.
findings.matters: End-of-life infrastructure replacement is non-deferrable capex. A finance director cannot cut this without risking service failure; a lender should understand this cannot be deferred if revenues tighten, making it a fixed cost on the council's budget.
findings.figures: Brocade LAN replacement £1,200,000; Cisco CPE replacement £150,000; Cisco IE3000 replacement £65,000; server infrastructure items totalling approximately £1,524,000
findings.quote: these switches are now approaching or have reached end-of-life (EOL) status, with limited vendor support, no firmware updates, and increasing hardware failure risk

findings.headline: Medway is borrowing £4.589m for ICT capital, with £3.209m due in 2026/27, concentrated in the first year.
findings.detail: The council's estimated capital program request totals £4,589,000 across five years, with 2026/27 requiring £3,209,000. Every item is proposed to be funded through borrowing, with no grants or third-party funding. This represents material new borrowing in a single year, front-loading debt service costs into the immediate revenue budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has sufficient revenue capacity and reserves to service this debt, and whether borrowing this much in one year creates stress on the budget if revenues soften. A finance director must confirm debt servicing capacity and repayment timing.

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate falls to 17.30%, below prior-year equivalent of 17.65%
findings.detail: Council tax collection at May 2026 is 17.30%, down 0.35 percentage points from 17.65% at the same point in 2025. The report notes collection rates have not returned to pre-pandemic levels, impacted by cost of living crisis, world events, and rising inflation.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates reduce in-year cash generation and increase borrowing need. Persistent weakness below pre-pandemic norms may reflect underlying deprivation or payment difficulties in the council's area.
findings.figures: 17.30% council tax collection (May 2026); down 0.35% from prior-year 17.65%; business rates 21.95% (up 1.94%)
findings.quote: As at May 2026 the council tax collection rate is 17.30%, which is 0.35% lower than the same month last year... Collection rates have not returned to pre-pandemic levels, impacted by the cost of living crisis, world events and rising inflation.

findings.headline: Children's services staffing overspend of £1.068m driven by market premium allowances and retention payments
findings.detail: Children's division is overspending by £1.068m on staffing due to paying above the budgeted midpoint salary and partly unbudgeted market premium allowances and retention payments. The council is using these to remain competitive with other local authorities and prevent permanent vacancies being filled by interim practitioners.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted staffing costs signal either budget-setting failure or genuine market tightness in recruitment. Either way, they indicate cost pressures outside the council's direct control and potential quality risk if interim staff become permanent.
findings.figures: £1.068m overspend on staffing; unbudgeted market premium allowances and retention payments
findings.quote: Reported £1.068m overspend on staffing across the division, principally due to the number of the employees in post being awarded higher than the budgeted midpoint salaries including the number of posts attracting the partly unbudgeted market premium allowances and retention payments.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements rising to 50 (vs budget 42), with individual costs reaching £15,000+/week
findings.detail: Children's services forecasts a £5.228m overspend after management action. External residential placements have risen to 50 against a budget of 42. Five placements cost over £10,000 per week; two exceed £15,000. Average cost is £7,781/week. The service is forecasting 8 additional placements before March 2027.
findings.matters: High-cost residential placements for children signal either service design problems, complexity in the cohort, or both. Placement costs that exceed budget by large margins with limited mitigation options indicate expenditure the council cannot control without difficult decisions about service levels.
findings.figures: 50 external residential placements (vs 42 budgeted); £7,781 average weekly cost; 5 placements over £10,000/week; 2 over £15,000/week; £5.228m overspend; 8 new placements forecast by March
findings.quote: the service is currently forecasting 50 external residential placements compared to the budgeted 42 places at an average cost of £7,781 a week... Five of the 50 placements are costing over £10,000 per week, two of which are over £15,000 a week.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation households and nightly rates both rising sharply
findings.detail: Homelessness and Temporary Accommodation is forecasting a £2.673m overspend. Households in TA rose from 472 in October 2023 to 631 by June 2026, and average nightly rates for private TA increased 30% (from £46 to £60 per unit) over 18 months. TA prevention costs, lost rental income on council-owned properties, and nightly TA demand are all under pressure.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in homelessness and accommodation costs signals both deprivation stress in the area and budget unpredictability. Councils with rising TA spend face years of pressure without policy change or housing supply intervention.
findings.figures: 631 households in TA (June 2026) vs 472 (Oct 2023); nightly rate £46→£60 (30% rise); £2.673m overspend; £1.5m pressure on nightly TA alone
findings.quote: The nightly TA numbers remain higher than in October 2023 when they were at a low of 472 and are currently reported at 631 at the end of June 2026. Alongside this the average nightly rate for private nightly TA has increased from £46 to £60 (30%) during the past eighteen months.

findings.headline: Interest rate assumption of 4.0% has proved wrong; actual rates near 5% creating £4.2m overspend
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumed PWLB interest rates would fall to 4.0%, but rates remain just below 5%. This creates a £4.162m overspend on the Interest and Financing budget. The council must refinance £150m of redeemable debt and fund £69m of capital expenditure from borrowing.
findings.matters: Sustained high borrowing costs erode a council's fiscal capacity and may force reductions in capital investment or service spending. Forecast volatility from interest rate misjudgement reduces predictability of the medium-term position.
findings.figures: £4.162m Interest & Financing overspend; budgeted at 4.0% PWLB rates, actual near 5%; £4.9m estimated pressure; £150m redeemable debt; £69m capital funded by borrowing
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget for Interest and Financing was set at £24.710m reflecting our assumption that PWLB interest rates would have reduced to around 4.0%. Global events affecting the economy mean that no longer looks likely and with average interest rates estimated to be just below 5% during 2026/27, this will result in a pressure on the Councils interest payable budget of just under £4.900m.

findings.headline: Adult social care cost growth of 12% year-on-year far exceeds funding assumptions
findings.detail: Adults services is forecasting an £18.695m overspend. Analysis shows package costs have risen 12% annually over the past three years, driven by both demand growth and increasing average weekly care costs. A £5.9m FIT plan saving remains undelivered; prior-year undelivered targets were rolled forward into this year's budget.
findings.matters: Structural cost inflation in social care that outpaces funding allocations signals whether a council can manage demand-led spending without successive years of budget pressures and savings shortfalls.
findings.figures: £18.695m overspend; 12% annual package cost growth; £5.900m FIT savings target; £133.200m gross cost of packages in 2025/26
findings.quote: Analysis of the last 3 financial years show that the average increase in total package costs have risen around 12% year on year... Undelivered savings targets from 2024/25 and 2025/26 were rolled forward in setting the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Forecast overspend of £26.7m exceeds council's £10m reserve cover
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £26.724m revenue overspend after management action, but holds only £10m in general reserves. This gap may force the council to seek Exceptional Financial Support from government. The overspend was £42.831m before £16.1m of proposed management actions.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund an overspend of this magnitude faces potential service cuts, forced borrowing, or loss of financial autonomy. Lenders assess council resilience partly by reserve adequacy relative to forecast volatility.
findings.figures: £26.724m overspend; £10.0m reserves; £42.831m before management action; 5.1% of £523.752m budget
findings.quote: The Council's general reserves currently stand at just over £10.0million. The Council would not therefore be in a position to fund an overspend on the scale of that currently projected.

findings.headline: Council has commenced regulatory and financial due diligence for transfer of another Registered Provider's housing portfolio into the HRA
findings.detail: The council is in early-stage due diligence for a proposed transfer of a Registered Provider's housing portfolio within the borough into the HRA. The paper describes this as 'a cost-effective opportunity to increase the Council's housing stock, ensure existing tenants benefit from safe and well-managed homes, and contribute to meeting future housing demand within Medway'. The transfer is subject to approval.
findings.matters: A portfolio transfer represents a significant change to the council's housing asset base and financial liabilities, with implications for borrowing capacity, debt servicing, and HRA business plan assumptions. Timing and cost of any transfer should be closely monitored.
findings.figures: Portfolio transfer under regulatory and financial due diligence; proposal stage only
findings.quote: Regulatory and financial due diligence has commenced in relation to the proposed transfer of a Registered Provider's housing portfolio within the borough into the HRA. Subject to approval, this transfer represents a cost-effective opportunity to increase the Council's housing stock

findings.headline: Complaints handling satisfaction dropped 7% and critical friend review of Housing Services complaints process completed in Q4
findings.detail: Overall tenant satisfaction rose by 4.5% in the 2025/26 TSM perception survey (573 respondents, 18.7% response rate). However, satisfaction decreased on 3 of 12 measures, with the most significant being a 7% drop in satisfaction with the approach to complaints handling. A critical friend review of complaints handling across Housing Services was completed in Q4, with findings to be used to enhance the complaints handling process and inform training for the coming year.
findings.matters: Declining satisfaction with complaints handling and the need for external critical friend review indicates weaknesses in tenant dispute resolution, which could escalate to Housing Ombudsman referrals or regulatory scrutiny given the council's existing C2 rating.
findings.figures: 7% drop in complaints handling satisfaction; 573 respondents (18.7% response rate); critical friend review completed Q4
findings.quote: A decrease in satisfaction was recorded on 3 of 12 measures, with the most statistically significant being the 7% drop in satisfaction with the approach to complaints handling. A critical friend review of complaints handling across the whole of Housing Services was completed in Q4.

findings.headline: Repairs backlog includes 332 overdue jobs out of 1,042 open repairs, with urgent and routine performance declining
findings.detail: Urgent and routine repairs performance slightly dropped compared to the previous year, with a slight increase in completion times and a small drop in appointments being kept. At year end there were 1,042 open repairs jobs, with 332 overdue. The paper notes that 'most outstanding cases had future appointments booked or were impacted by tenant availability and resource constraints'. Performance is actively managed through regular contractor reporting and review.
findings.matters: A growing repairs backlog with nearly a third of jobs overdue suggests capacity constraints and could indicate potential Service failures that might attract regulatory or legal challenge, particularly given the council's C2 rating for landlord services.
findings.figures: 1,042 open repairs jobs at year end; 332 overdue (31.8%); urgent and routine repairs performance 'slightly dropped'
findings.quote: At year end there were 1,042 open repairs jobs, with 332 overdue. Although levels reduced from Q3, most outstanding cases had future appointments booked or were impacted by tenant availability and resource constraints, with performance actively managed through regular contractor reporting and review.

findings.headline: Roofing planned maintenance programme showing zero completion for blocks, with delays attributed to S20 approvals and access issues
findings.detail: Within the 18-month planned works programme that concluded 31 March 2026, roofing is identified as 'the main delivery concern'. Pitched roofs to houses achieved only 23.2% completion, blocks at 0% completion (pending S20), and flat roofs at 50%. These delays are attributed to late starts, access issues, and earlier commercial constraints. A new programme is underway for 2026/27. Overall, 2,526 of 3,464 live elements were completed in 2025/26 (72.9%).
findings.matters: Roofing delays and zero completion for block roofing indicate capital programme slippage and potential ongoing maintenance backlogs. Blocks at 0% completion pending S20 (leaseholder) approval may indicate governance complexity in the council's housing portfolio.
findings.figures: Blocks roofing 0% complete; pitched roofs to houses 23.2%; flat roofs 50%; overall programme 72.9% complete against live scope; over £3.5m delivered against capital budget
findings.quote: Mears – roofing: Roofing remains the main delivery concern, with pitched roofs to houses at 23.2%, blocks at 0% (pending S20), and flat roofs at 50%, reflecting late starts, access issues, and earlier commercial constraints. These have now been addressed and a programme is underway on 2026/27.

findings.headline: Rent arrears rising with half of HRA tenants at risk of further increases from Universal Credit migration
findings.detail: Current rent arrears at end of Q4 were 1.14% compared to 1.06% at the end of the previous financial year. Approximately 1,602 HRA tenants (about 50% of HRA tenancies) are being migrated from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit, which the council acknowledges 'carries risk of an increase'. Tenancy sustainment supported over £150k in payments to rent accounts, and the Household Support Fund is being replaced by the Crisis and Resilience Fund.
findings.matters: Rising arrears and acknowledged risks from UC migration could indicate deteriorating financial performance in the HRA, which is ringfenced but still reflects tenant payment capacity and the council's ability to sustain housing services revenue.
findings.figures: 1.14% arrears (Q4 year-end) vs 1.06% previous year; 1,602 tenants (50% of tenancies) migrating to UC; £150k tenancy sustainment payments
findings.quote: Current rent arrears at the end of Q4 were at 1.14% compared to 1.06% at the end of the previous financial year. An Increasing number of HRA tenants are being migrated from HB to UC (1602 tenants – approx. 50% of HRA tenancies) which carries risk of an increase

findings.headline: Council received C2 regulatory rating from housing regulator and is working to reach C1
findings.detail: Medway Council underwent a programmed inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing between June and September 2024 and received a C2 grade, announced in November 2024. The council has created a continuous improvement action plan and continues quarterly engagement with the Regulator. The next meeting is scheduled for 18 June, with work ongoing to provide evidence and reassurance to seek a regrade to C1 status.
findings.matters: A C2 rating from the social housing regulator indicates regulatory concern about landlord services and may signal governance weaknesses that could affect the council's creditworthiness and borrowing terms.
findings.figures: C2 grade awarded November 2024; monthly engagement reduced to quarterly as of April 2025
findings.quote: The Regulatory Judgement published in November 2024 awarded Medway Council a C2 grade. Continued engagement with the Regulator is ongoing quarterly against the continuous improvement plan. The next meeting with the Regulator is scheduled for 18th June and work is ongoing to provide evidence and reassurance to seek a regrade of C1 status.

findings.headline: The council has committed to capital investment in acquired homes for energy efficiency, targeting EPC C by 2030 and net zero by 2050
findings.detail: Beyond the £45m acquisition cost, the council is integrating these homes into its HRA Asset and Energy Strategy, committing to further capital investment for energy efficiency improvements to meet net zero targets by 2050.
findings.matters: This commitment requires additional capital investment post-acquisition, increasing total cost of ownership and long-term capital requirements for the HRA.
findings.figures: EPC C compliance by 2030, net zero carbon by 2050
findings.quote: the acquired properties will be incorporated into the Council's HRA Asset and Energy Strategy, supporting the delivery of EPC C compliance by 2030 and the Council's commitment to achieving net zero carbon by 2050. Over time, planned investment in these homes will improve energy efficiency, reduce carbon emissions, and lower energy costs for residents.

findings.headline: The acquisition's financial viability depends on variables including stock condition, rental income, and borrowing rates
findings.detail: Savills have completed initial financial modelling confirming viability, but the council's risk register explicitly identifies that variances in stock condition, rental income, or borrowing rates could impact viability. This indicates the financial case is sensitive to these factors.
findings.matters: If rental income or borrowing rates move adversely, the acquisition's economics could deteriorate significantly, affecting HRA sustainability.
findings.figures: Risk rating B2 (Likely/Major impact)
findings.quote: Variances in stock condition, rental income, or borrowing rates could impact viability.

findings.headline: Medway is proceeding with a £45 million HRA acquisition of 791 homes from a registered provider
findings.detail: Full Council approved this capital acquisition in April 2026 and the council is now moving to delivery phase by appointing specialist advisors. The acquisition will bring 791 homes into the HRA and represents a significant expansion of the council's housing stock.
findings.matters: A £45m acquisition expands the HRA's asset and liability base materially, affecting debt service requirements, HRA reserves, and long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: c.£45m acquisition, 791 homes
findings.quote: This report seeks approval to directly appoint Savills as specialist advisor/consultant to support the acquisition of 791 homes from London & Quadrant (L&Q) into the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). The acquisition (c.£45m) has been approved by Full Council (April 2026).

findings.headline: Expected revenue savings from infrastructure consolidation and SOC services are noted but not quantified, leaving the net cost to the council unclear.
findings.detail: The paper states that 'some elements, such as the Security Operations Centre (SOC) and KPSN circuit consolidation, are expected to deliver ongoing revenue savings, helping offset operational costs.' The benefits register mentions 'cost avoidance through circuit consolidation and support savings' but no figures are provided for these offsets. This means the annual interest cost of £82,000+ may not be fully offset by the savings claimed.
findings.matters: The business case for borrowing rests partly on cost recovery through operational savings, but these are unquantified; if not realised, the council faces ongoing budget pressure to cover interest costs.
findings.figures: £82,000 annual interest cost (2026/27); expected savings unspecified; SOC investment £580,000; KPSN circuit consolidation savings: not quantified
findings.quote: Some elements, such as the Security Operations Centre (SOC) and KPSN circuit consolidation, are expected to deliver ongoing revenue savings, helping offset operational costs.

findings.headline: Programme funding is explicitly limited to 2026–2028 due to Local Government Reorganisation, leaving the final three years' funding and governance arrangements undefined.
findings.detail: Section 9.2 states: 'Due to LGR we will be only seeking Capital borrowing to support the program of works for years 2026 to 2028.' This creates a two-part funding structure with the post-LGR position for 2028–2031 unresolved. The paper acknowledges the programme must be 'future-proofed' for the new authority structure but does not clarify which council will own the infrastructure or fund the remaining investment.
findings.matters: The programme spans five years but is only funded/governed through the first three; this creates uncertainty about completion, cost allocation, and which entity will be responsible for the assets post-merger.
findings.figures: Five-year programme (2026–2031); only three years funded (2026–2028); total estimated cost exceeds £3.5m over full period
findings.quote: Due to LGR we will be only seeking Capital borrowing to support the program of works for years 2026 to 2028.

findings.headline: Cabinet is requesting £3.869m in prudential borrowing for ICT infrastructure refresh, but has not yet identified funding for borrowing interest costs beyond 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper explicitly recommends adding £3,869,000 to the Capital Programme funded by prudential borrowing. Section 9.2 states the council must 'identify savings to support the £82,000 interest costs for 2026/27' and will 'review budgets for 2027/28 to cover the interest costs for 2027/28', indicating no committed funding for these costs in year two. The programme is structured only through 2028 due to Local Government Reorganisation, leaving the funding position for 2028–2031 unclear.
findings.matters: This is a material capital commitment where the council is borrowing £3.869m without a confirmed funding plan for interest costs in year two, creating a potential budget pressure in 2027/28 ahead of organisational restructuring.
findings.figures: £3,869,000 capital borrowing; £82,000 interest costs in 2026/27; borrowing only planned for 2026–2028; total programme cost exceeds £3.5 million over five years
findings.quote: The Cabinet is requested to recommend to full Council the addition of £3,869,000 to the Capital Programme to be funded by prudential borrowing. ... ICT to identify savings to support the £82,000 interest costs for 2026/27 and review budgets for 2027/28 to cover the interest costs for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Property disposals generated £18–19m in proceeds, with £13.6m allocated to debt repayment rather than capital investment
findings.detail: The council realized £18–19m from property sales. Of this, only £2.9m was used for transformation, £1m for capital programme, and critically, £13.6m went directly to debt repayment. This reallocation of proceeds away from capital investment toward debt service suggests cash flow pressure and a need to reduce borrowing burden.
findings.matters: Diverting property sale proceeds to debt repayment rather than capital reinvestment indicates the council is managing cash strain rather than investing in future income-generating assets
findings.figures: Property disposals £18–19m; debt repayment £13.6m; transformation budget £2.9m; capital programme £1m
findings.quote: £18m-£19m had been realised and £2.9m had been used as capital receipts as part of the transformation budget. £1m had been added to the capital programme and £13.6m allocated to debt

findings.headline: Grant Thornton's review of Medway Development Company's financial resilience has reached no conclusion, leaving £153.4m subsidiary loan exposure uncertain
findings.detail: The council holds £153.4m in loans to Medway Development Company, its property development subsidiary. A member of the Audit Committee flagged concerns about MDC's financial resilience at previous meetings. The Chief Operating Officer confirmed that cashflow analysis had been completed and provided to Grant Thornton, but 'no conclusion had yet been reached,' leaving the status of this major exposure unresolved.
findings.matters: An unresolved Grant Thornton review of a £153.4m subsidiary exposure suggests potential financial distress; if the subsidiary fails, the council's losses could be substantial
findings.figures: £153.4m in loans to subsidiaries; £17.5m directly owned property
findings.quote: The Chief Operating Officer stated that the cashflow analysis he requested had been undertaken and provided to Grant Thornton, however no conclusion had yet been reached.

findings.headline: £20m of LOBO loans face potential call within 12 months, with refinancing costs of £60k–£130k depending on how many are called in
findings.detail: Four LOBO (Lender Option, Borrower Option) loans carrying rates of 3.6%–4.75% may be called in by lenders within the next 12 months. If the lowest-rate loan at 3.6% is called and refinanced at current market rates, annual costs rise by approximately £60k. If all four loans are called in, the annual cost pressure reaches £130k.
findings.matters: LOBO call dates represent refinancing risk at higher rates, adding unexpected debt servicing costs that further compress already-tight finances
findings.figures: £20m of LOBO loans at risk; potential cost pressures £60,000 (one loan) to £130,000 (all four)
findings.quote: If that loan was called in, the additional costs associated with a higher interest rate would add a pressure of around £60,000. If all four loans were called in, further borrowing would be taken at today's rates which would add a pressure of £130,000 to the budget.

findings.headline: Net borrowing jumped £118m in a single year to £534m, driven by capital spending, exceptional financial support, and Medway Development Company
findings.detail: Total loans held reached £714m at 31 March 2026, up £130m from the prior year. Net borrowing rose from £416.4m to £534.4m. The Chief Operating Officer noted this was driven by significant capital expenditure, exceptional financial support needs, and ongoing investment in the subsidiary Medway Development Company.
findings.matters: Rapid debt accumulation of this scale increases financial risk, constrains future borrowing capacity, and suggests either major capital commitments or financial distress requiring exceptional support
findings.figures: Net borrowing increase £118m; total loans £714m (up £130m); External borrowing £713.535m
findings.quote: The significant movements in borrowing are because of significant capital expenditure, the need for exceptional financial support and ongoing capital investment in Medway Development Company.

findings.headline: Interest and financing costs overshot budget by £6.3m due to rising rates and a budget build error
findings.detail: Interest paid reached £28.591m against a budget of £22.381m. The budget had assumed interest rates would fall, but instead they rose. An error in budget preparation that omitted some borrowing provisions compounded the problem. The council acknowledged this forecasting failure created material unbudgeted finance pressure.
findings.matters: A £6.3m overspend on finance costs signals either weak budget forecasting or structural underfunding of debt servicing, both of which concern lenders about financial resilience
findings.figures: Interest paid £28.591m (budget £22.381m), variance £6.210m; Interest budget deficit £5.853m against total Interest and Financing budget of £23.960m
findings.quote: the budget for 2025/26 had made assumptions that interest rates would fall, however this had not been the case, interest rates went up, this was exacerbated by an error in the budget build which had omitted some borrowing. Therefore, more borrowing at a higher cost than predicted was required leading to the overspend on the finance and interest budget of £6.3m for the year.

findings.headline: £45.95m new HRA housing acquisition scheme added post-budget dependent on due diligence outcomes with completion timing uncertain (early 2027/28).
findings.detail: A major acquisition of approximately 791 properties from a registered provider's portfolio was approved in April 2026 after the February budget. Due diligence is occurring in 2026/27 with acquisition completion contingent on satisfaction of that work and expected 'early in 2027/28'. This substantially expands the borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: This represents a material addition to the council's borrowing programme post-budget; both the final cost and the timing are conditional, creating exposure if due diligence raises concerns about value or feasibility.
findings.figures: £45.950 million, approximately 791 properties, early 2027/28 completion contingent on due diligence
findings.quote: to acquire stock located in Medway from a registered provider's portfolio. It comprises approximately 791 properties. Due diligence work, including expert analysis and valuations, are forecast for this financial year. If satisfied, acquisition is expected early in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Multiple major capital schemes are already forecasting cost pressures at early design stages, suggesting inflationary risk across the programme.
findings.detail: Danecourt Secondary Expansion (£24.967m) is forecasting a £613k overspend at early design stage; All Saints Primary SEN indicates additional funding will be required; Brook Theatre (£16.703m) discovered 'serious structural issues' forcing schedule extension to spring 2028; Gun Wharf Improvement Works requires 'value engineering required to keep costs within budget'.
findings.matters: Early cost overruns and structural discoveries on major schemes suggest the council's cost estimates may be under-pressure; this pattern across multiple schemes raises the risk of further funding requests before completion.
findings.figures: £24.967 million (Danecourt), £613,000 overspend, £16.703 million (Brook Theatre), spring 2028 completion (delayed from earlier dates)
findings.quote: The project is at the early design stage but there are already indications that the scheme may cost more than initially expected. The scheme is currently forecasting an overspend of £613,000

findings.headline: Capital programme is 71% funded by prudential borrowing with interest rate risk flagged as Likely/Major by the council itself.
findings.detail: The approved capital programme totals £308.222m, of which £218.812m is funded through borrowing. The council's own risk register identifies that if interest rates exceed budgeted levels, there will be negative impact on the Interest and financing budget, rated B2 (Likely/Major impact).
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate council balance sheets for debt servicing risk; interest rate sensitivity at this scale and likelihood rating indicates the council considers this a material near-term exposure.
findings.figures: £218.812 million borrowing from £308.222 million total; £218,812k of £308,222k approved budget
findings.quote: A large proportion of the capital budget is funded from borrowing. If interest rates are in excess of that budgeted for, this may have a negative impact upon the Council's Interest and financing budget.

findings.paper_title: Amendments to the Revenue Budget and Capital Programme
findings.headline: £7m committed to Local Government Reorganisation over 2026–28, funded from capital receipts that might otherwise support capital investment
findings.detail: The council will spend £3m in 2026/27 and £3m in 2027/28 on internal LGR resources, plus £1m contribution to the county-wide Programme Management Office. The new unitary arrangements go live in April 2028. Funding comes from capital receipts under government flexibilities.
findings.matters: These costs divert capital receipts away from capital investment and create substantial financial demands during the transition period. The council must deliver day-to-day services while absorbing significant transformation overhead, which may constrain borrowing capacity or capital delivery.
findings.figures: £3.0m (2026/27); £3.0m (2027/28); £1.0m county-wide PMO; £7.0m total from capital receipts
findings.quote: Internal resources in 2026/27 £3.0 million Internal resources in 2027/28 £3.0 million Contribution towards the county-wide PMO £1.0 million TOTAL CAPITAL RECEIPTS REQUIRED £7.0 million

findings.paper_title: Amendments to the Revenue Budget and Capital Programme
findings.headline: General reserves depleted to £10.012m, matching the Section 151 Officer's minimum threshold, leaving no buffer
findings.detail: The council is using £3.743m from general reserves to fund the 2025/26 outturn, reducing reserves from £13.805m to £10.012m. This final balance sits at or marginally above the Section 151 Officer's minimum threshold of £10m, eliminating any financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Reserves at minimum provide no cushion for emergencies or unexpected costs. Any future overspend, service demand spike, or unforeseen liability will force immediate corrective action or borrowing, reducing the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £3.743m used from reserves; £10.012m final balance; £10m minimum threshold
findings.quote: use a total of £3.743million of the available reserves; taking the balance to £10.012million

findings.paper_title: Amendments to the Revenue Budget and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £14.695m was the principal cause of the council's overall £9.819m revenue outturn deficit
findings.detail: ASC overspent by £14.695m in 2025/26, representing the primary driver of the council's overall revenue shortfall. The paper acknowledges this mirrors challenges across almost all upper tier authorities, but does not explain how the council plans to address the ongoing demand pressure.
findings.matters: This level of overspend indicates structural demand pressure that is difficult to control through one-off savings. If ASC spending remains at this level, the council will face persistent budget pressure and continued reliance on reserves or further corrective action.
findings.figures: £14.695m Adult Social Care overspend; £9.819m net revenue overspend overall
findings.quote: the principal cause of this is the £14.695million overspend against Adult Social Care, mirroring the challenge confronted by almost all upper tier authorities across the country

findings.headline: Liquid cash reserves collapsed from £14.3m to £84k, eliminating financial buffer.
findings.detail: Cash and cash equivalents fell from £14.256m at the start of the year to just £84k by 31 March 2026, a reduction of 99.4%. Total investments also fell by £25.169m net. The council now has virtually no immediate liquidity reserves.
findings.matters: Near-zero cash reserves eliminate the council's ability to smooth cash flows or absorb unexpected spending shocks without immediately drawing on expensive short-term borrowing.
findings.figures: Cash and cash equivalents: £84k (from £14.256m opening). Total investments net draw-down: £25.169m
findings.quote: Cash and cash equivalents 14,256 (14,173) 84

findings.headline: £20m of LOBO loans have call dates within 12 months, creating rate escalation risk.
findings.detail: The council holds £20m in LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans with embedded call options exercisable within the next 12 months. If the lender exercises the option and proposes higher rates, the council must either accept the increase or repay.
findings.matters: LOBO loans are a contingent liability; lender-initiated rate increases could force unexpected cost growth or forced refinancing at exactly the time when short-term rates have risen to 5-7%.
findings.figures: LOBO loans with 12-month call dates: £20m. Total LOBO portfolio: £50.5m
findings.quote: The Authority has £20m LOBO loans with call dates within the next 12 months. If the option is exercised and an increased rate proposed. If required, the Authority will repay the LOBO loans with available cash or by borrowing from other local authorities or the PWLB.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing doubled to £184.5m with refinancing costs accelerating towards year-end.
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing increased from £90.001m to £184.500m, more than doubling in a year. The weighted average rate increased from 4.73% to 4.85%. Market rates for short-term borrowing spiked significantly at year-end, creating refinancing pressure.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on short-term refinancing exposes the council to rate spikes; a 1% rate rise on £184.5m costs an additional £1.8m annually in servicing costs.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing: £184.5m at 4.85% average (from £90m at 4.73%). Year-end market rates: 5.0%-7.0%
findings.quote: rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0% being seen.

findings.headline: External borrowing jumped £129.5m to £713.5m, largely for capital expenditure and Medway Development Company investments.
findings.detail: Total external borrowing increased from £584.035m to £713.535m, driven by capital programmes and non-core investments. The Capital Financing Requirement rose by £90.081m. The council holds £153.4m in loans to subsidiaries, which appears to be financing the development company.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth strains long-term revenue affordability; commercial investment in subsidiaries carries additional risk and is harder for lenders to assess than core service borrowing.
findings.figures: External borrowing: £713.535m (up £129.5m from £584.035m). CFR: £676.115m. Loans to subsidiaries: £153.4m
findings.quote: The significant movements in borrowing are because of significant capital expenditure, the need for exceptional financial support and ongoing capital investment in Medway Development Company.

findings.headline: Interest costs exceeded budget by £6.2m (27%), driven by higher-than-expected borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Interest paid was £28.591m against a budget of £22.381m, creating a variance of £6.210m. The overall Interest and Financing budget deficit was £5.853m above target. Rising interest rates during the year, combined with higher debt levels, drove costs above the planned budget.
findings.matters: Interest cost overshoots reduce the council's revenue flexibility and ability to fund services; they signal budget forecasting issues or unexpected cost drivers.
findings.figures: Interest Paid: £28.591m vs budget £22.381m (£6.210m variance). Total Interest & Financing: £23.960m vs budget £18.107m
findings.quote: Overall, the Interest and Financing budget made a deficit of £5.853million over its targeted budget of £18.107million.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report, Audit Findings Report and Statement of Accounts 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor identifies significant weakness in governance of financial reporting and audit support processes
findings.detail: Grant Thornton found a significant weakness in Governance related to preparing draft accounts and supporting the audit. The council had delayed delivery of detailed working papers and evidence; finance teams were managing monthly budget monitoring during the testing phase; staff absences from long-term sickness impacted audit query response times. The draft Statement of Accounts published in May 2025 contained quality issues requiring correction, and Group Accounts were not included because a subsidiary failed to provide information within the agreed timetable.
findings.matters: Weak financial reporting governance and inadequate internal controls mean the council's true financial position cannot be reliably assessed. Poor audit readiness indicates insufficient systems and processes for financial management and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Quality issues identified in draft accounts; Group Accounts missing from draft publication
findings.quote: Governance – Significant weakness identified in relation to preparing draft accounts and supporting the audit process, one key recommendation made.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report, Audit Findings Report and Statement of Accounts 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor identifies significant weakness in the council's ability to achieve a balanced budget
findings.detail: The Value for Money assessment found a significant weakness in Financial Sustainability specifically relating to achieving a balanced budget. One key recommendation and two improvement recommendations were issued. The council's response notes that 2024-25 budget setting included provisions for right-sizing, but the finance team suffered long-term sickness during the budget monitoring period.
findings.matters: A council demonstrating structural inability to achieve balanced budgets represents material credit risk. This suggests weak financial planning, inadequate savings delivery, or underlying deficits that could impair debt service capacity.
findings.figures: One key recommendation and two improvement recommendations on financial sustainability
findings.quote: Financial Sustainability – Significant weakness identified for achieving a balanced budget, one key and two improvement recommendations made.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report, Audit Findings Report and Statement of Accounts 2024/25
findings.headline: Grant Thornton issues disclaimer opinion on 2024/25 accounts for fourth consecutive year
findings.detail: The auditor cannot express an opinion on whether the financial statements present a true and fair view. This continues a pattern of disclaimer opinions for 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24. Reasons cited include delays in producing working papers, finance teams simultaneously undertaking monthly budget monitoring during the audit, staff long-term sickness, and a subsidiary's failure to provide group account information within the agreed timeframe.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on audited accounts as verification of the council's financial position if the auditor disclaims responsibility. This is fundamental to credit assessment and materially limits confidence in reported financial data.
findings.quote: The result of this Audit is the same as those given for 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 which is a Disclaimer opinion.

findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of audit disclaimer due to backstop legislation and incomplete testing
findings.detail: Medway has been subject to backstop disclaimer since 2021/22. For 2024/25, the auditor closed fieldwork on 16 January 2026 without completing in-year transaction testing, determining it impossible to finish before the 27 February 2026 statutory deadline. The auditor will issue a disclaimer of opinion, unable to form an opinion on the financial statements.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess financial position or trajectory when the auditor cannot provide assurance. Four consecutive disclaimers indicate systemic audit collapse, not transient delay.
findings.figures: Backdated disclaimers: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, and anticipated 2024/25
findings.quote: The Authority has been subject to a backstop disclaimer of audit opinion on the financial statements since 2021/22, with 2022/23 and 2023/24 also being subject to disclaimer of audit opinions under these arrangements.

findings.headline: Council Tax frozen in real terms at 4.994% increase but request for additional flexibility above referendum threshold was refused by government
findings.detail: The council requested flexibility to increase Council Tax above the 3% core threshold plus 2% Adult Social Care precept (total 5%), citing budget pressures. The government refused this request in the Final Settlement.
findings.matters: Shows government is not granting additional revenue flexibility to Medway, constraining income options. The council is maximizing standard referendum powers but still has a gap.
findings.figures: 4.994% increase approved (3% core + 1.994% social care); request for additional flexibility rejected
findings.quote: For Medway Council, this represents a core referendum threshold of up to 3% per year and as a local authority with social care responsibilities, the ability to set an Adult Social Care Precept of 2% per year without a referendum...the Council made a request to the Government through the EFS scheme for flexibility to increase the Council Tax above the referendum threshold, however the Final Settlement confirmed that Medway's request had not been granted.

findings.headline: S151 Officer expresses discomfort with reserves adequacy but expresses confidence budget is 'robust'
findings.detail: In the Section 25 statement, the Chief Operating Officer (S151 Officer) states 'the Council's reserves remain below a level that I would be comfortable with' and acknowledges the council was 'poorly served by the local government finance system for many years'. However, notes the Fair Funding Review 2.0 should mean this is the last budget requiring EFS.
findings.matters: The CFO is flagging discomfort with the reserve position, which is a formal statement of risk for external parties. This is a cautionary signal despite expressing robustness.
findings.figures: None specific, but relates to 2% reserve level vs. 5% target
findings.quote: As the Section 151 Officer, I would prefer that the Council were not reliant on exceptional financial support to balance its budget and the Council's reserves remain below a level that I would be comfortable with, however the positive impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and the certainty provided by a three year settlement, inspires confidence that this will be the last budget that this Council has to set with recourse to exceptional financial support.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £1.771 million carried into 2026/27 from business rates shortfall
findings.detail: Business rates collected in 2025/26 fell short of budget, creating a deficit that must be absorbed in 2026/27. Separately, the council has implemented a 0.25% reduction in Council Tax collection rate due to cost-of-living pressures.
findings.matters: Shows deterioration in the council's own-source income base and resident payment difficulties. Both suggest weakening local economic conditions.
findings.figures: £1.771m business rates collection fund deficit; 0.25% reduction in Council Tax collection rate
findings.quote: At the end of the 2025/26 financial year there was a deficit on the collection fund of £1.771million which Medway can budget for in 2026/27. This calculation reflects the impact of a projected 0.25% reduction in the collection rate due to the continued impact of the cost-of-living crisis on collection.

findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG deficit not projected to clear until end of 2026/27, despite Safety Valve scheme
findings.detail: The High Needs Block cumulative deficit is £9.998m at start of 2026/27. Although a new High Needs Stability Grant has been announced, the deficit reflects structural SEND spending exceeding available grant funding.
findings.matters: SEND is a volatile, growing cost area. Even with government support, it reveals mismatch between statutory duties and funding.
findings.figures: Opening deficit 2026/27: £9.998m; projected to reach small surplus (£70k) by end of 2027/28
findings.quote: The introduction of the High needs stability grant means that the council is expected to achieve a surplus position by the end of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation funding pressure of £2.088 million in 2026/27
findings.detail: Cost of providing temporary accommodation to homeless households is accelerating. This reflects national housing crisis and cost-of-living impact on residents.
findings.matters: Demand-led spending that continues to grow, indicative of broader socioeconomic stress in the area and population vulnerability.
findings.figures: £2.088 million pressure in 2026/27
findings.quote: The projections include the funding of a £2.088million pressure relating to the provision of Temporary Accommodation.

findings.headline: Interest and Financing budget increased by £3.515 million; 64% of capital programme funded through borrowing
findings.detail: Higher PWLB rates and increased borrowing for capital projects and MDC lending have pushed interest costs up sharply. The council no longer has sufficient cash balances to self-fund operations.
findings.matters: Shows debt service climbing and erosion of the council's internal liquidity. Continued reliance on external borrowing at elevated rates is a structural weakness.
findings.figures: £24.710m total Interest & Financing budget (up £3.515m); 64% of £229.722m capital programme funded through borrowing
findings.quote: Around 64% of the Council's existing capital programme of £229.722million is funded through borrowing and interest rates continue to be higher than previously projected resulting in a budget pressure. The Council also previously borrowed from other local authorities, however the EFS agreed has resulted in a perception of higher risk, resulting in elevated rates compared to the PWLB.

findings.headline: £44 million care home development scheme adds £2.7 million annual financing cost
findings.detail: Full Council approved borrowing for a Medway-owned care home at Innovation Park Medway South in October 2025. This long-term commitment increases Interest & Financing budget materially and represents new debt on the books.
findings.matters: Major capital project increases ongoing debt service burden. Risk depends on care home business model returns and occupancy assumptions.
findings.figures: £44 million total borrowing; £2.7 million annual interest/financing cost in 2026/27
findings.quote: On 16 October 2025 Full Council agreed the addition of a total of up to £44million to the Council's capital programme for the development of a Medway Council owned and operated care home at Innovation Park Medway (IPM) South. This scheme adds £2.7million a year to the budget requirement for Interest and Financing

findings.headline: Adult Social Care budget pressures £7.629m, driven by placement costs exceeding budget by £7.596m
findings.detail: The primary driver is cost of current service pressure (placements in excess of budget), plus demographic growth of 3% adding £3.137m. The council is legally obliged to provide care regardless of whether it can afford it.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is demand-led and practically non-negotiable; it is one of the largest budget pressures and directly reflects demographic trends the council cannot control.
findings.figures: £7.629m total increase; £7.596m placement cost pressure; £3.137m demographic growth
findings.quote: The primary drivers are the cost of placements in excess of the current year budget (referred to as the cost of current service pressure) of £7.596million and uplifts of £3.902million (broadly 3% a year across the medium term) to progress towards the fair cost of care

findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) already projected to overspend by £9.985 million
findings.detail: Despite budget setting, the council is forecasting it will spend nearly £10m more than budgeted in 2025/26, even after declassifying £2.285m of earmarked reserves. This feeds into EFS requests.
findings.matters: Shows the council is not controlling expenditure to budget, a material risk for lenders assessing financial management capability.
findings.figures: £9.985 million projected overspend for 2025/26
findings.quote: The Round 3 revenue budget monitoring report presented to Cabinet on 10 February 2026 projects that the Council will overspend by £9.985million, even after declassifying £2.285million of earmarked reserves

findings.headline: General fund reserves have collapsed to just 2% of budget requirement, well below the 5% target
findings.detail: Non-earmarked reserves fell from £26.551m (7.5% of budget) in March 2022 to £10.061m (2% of budget) by March 2025. The council has been unable to set budgets without drawing on reserves for years.
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council has minimal capacity to absorb emergencies, overspends, or income shocks. The S151 Officer states reserves are 'below a level that I would be comfortable with'.
findings.figures: Non-earmarked reserves March 2025: £10.061m; target level (5%): approximately £26.2m
findings.quote: by March 2025 non-earmarked general fund reserves had fallen back to just over £10.0million, which represents around 2.0% of the 2025/26 budget requirement

findings.headline: Council requires £9.856 million Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The budget gap means Medway must seek capitalisation direction (borrowing for revenue purposes) for the third consecutive year. The S151 Officer previously noted uncertainty about whether this would be the last such request.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot balance its budget without government subsidy, suggesting structural imbalance and dependency on policy decisions outside its control.
findings.figures: £9.856 million EFS required for 2026/27; £18.184 million already received in 2025/26
findings.quote: In order to fund the budget gap projected in this proposed Budget, it would be necessary to request an additional £9.856million EFS for 2026/27 and the Proposed Budget reflects the inclusion of borrowing to support this.

findings.headline: Local Government Reform in next two years will transfer debt to successor authority
findings.detail: Local Government Reform is scheduled for the next two years, after which Medway Council will cease to exist and debt will transfer to a successor authority. The Council argues that capital assets and programme benefits will also transfer, but there is structural uncertainty about successor authority's appetite for inherited debt and capital commitments.
findings.matters: Debt succession risk: lenders need certainty that the successor authority will honour inherited obligations and support capital schemes. Reform creates governance uncertainty during a period of rising debt.
findings.figures: Reform scheduled within two years
findings.quote: Local Government Reform scheduled to take place over the next two years with a successor authority being responsible for the debt

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support repayment committed over 20 years
findings.detail: The Council has received Exceptional Financial Support borrowing which must be repaid according to MRP guidance over 20 years. This is a long-term revenue commitment that will constrain the Council's flexibility.
findings.matters: EFS repayment is a mandatory long-term liability that reduces revenue flexibility for decades; if the Council's revenue position deteriorates, this fixed obligation creates strain.
findings.figures: 20-year repayment period
findings.quote: The guidance required payment of the EFS over two twenty years

findings.headline: Large fixed-rate loan to subsidiaries: £125m exposure
findings.detail: The Council has a £125m fixed-rate loan to subsidiaries (PSR loans). While the Council confirmed it had not breached upper limits, this is a material concentration of credit exposure to a subsidiary entity, creating counterparty risk.
findings.matters: Subsidiary lending creates counterparty risk; if the subsidiary's financial position deteriorates, the Council's credit position is directly affected.
findings.figures: £125m fixed-rate loan to subsidiaries
findings.quote: the fixed rate loan was £125m

findings.headline: External borrowing expected to increase over the next three years
findings.detail: The Head of Corporate Accounts envisioned external borrowing rising over the next three years, meaning the Council is not planning to reduce reliance on market borrowing and will need to access debt markets repeatedly.
findings.matters: Sustained borrowing need means the Council remains exposed to market conditions and credit spreads; if borrowing costs rise, it flows directly into revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Increase envisioned over next three years
findings.quote: It is envisioned that external borrowing would increase over the next three years

findings.headline: Debt maturity profile concentrated in next two to three years
findings.detail: The Council's debt repayment is weighted toward the next 2-3 years before falling. This concentration creates refinancing risk — a large volume of debt maturing at the same time, when interest rates and market conditions may be unfavourable.
findings.matters: Concentrated debt maturity creates refinancing risk and limits options if market conditions worsen or rates spike during the peak repayment window.
findings.figures: Peak maturity window: next 2-3 years
findings.quote: The Debt Maturity profile shows debt repayment to peak over the next two to three years, before falling

findings.headline: Debt expanding sharply: £80m increase this year, £120m planned for next
findings.detail: The Council has already increased debt by £80m in the current financial year and is planning a further £120m increase in 2026/27. Members raised concern about this trajectory, but the Chief Operating Officer acknowledged the rise while defending it as linked to growth in Council assets and capital programme benefits accruing over the long term.
findings.matters: Rapid debt expansion limits financial flexibility and increases refinancing risk, especially critical if interest rates remain elevated or rise further.
findings.figures: £80m increase this financial year; £120m planned increase next year
findings.quote: the debt had increased by £80m this financial year and was planned to increase by £120m next year

findings.paper_title: Corporate debt and Council Tax Discretionary Policies
findings.headline: £300k of previously written-off Council Tax debt was recovered in 2025/26 through improved address-matching technology
findings.detail: The Pathway platform, deployed in December 2025 with Credit Reference Agency data and Open Banking insights, provided updated contact address data that enabled recovery of £300k in previously written-off debt. This indicates past collection losses that went unrecovered until new technology was deployed.
findings.matters: The recovery demonstrates both historical collection weakness (significant write-offs) and current improvements in recovery capability. For lenders, this indicates whether the council's collection performance is stable or improving.
findings.figures: £300k recovered in 2025/26
findings.quote: the platform provides updated contact address data, which enabled us to reverse £300k of previously written-off debt in 2025/26 by locating residents at new addresses.

findings.paper_title: Corporate debt and Council Tax Discretionary Policies
findings.headline: Council Tax funding is growing as a proportion of total council income
findings.detail: The paper states that Council Tax has become vital to the council's budget, with its proportion of funding increasing over time. This growing reliance on Council Tax creates revenue concentration risk, particularly given the council is now formalizing policies for vulnerable residents and those in financial difficulty.
findings.matters: For lenders, growing reliance on Council Tax (dependent on resident payment capacity) is a revenue stability concern compared to government grants. The council is managing income from an increasingly vulnerable resident base.
findings.figures: Not quantified; stated as a trend
findings.quote: Council Tax is a vital source of income for the Council with the proportion of funding increasing over time.

findings.headline: £17.8m invested in illiquid property funds with potential capital loss and redemption restrictions
findings.detail: The council holds £17.8m in externally managed property funds (10.73% of treasury investments as at 14 Jan 2026). These are described as having minimum 5-7 year timeframes, with potential for capital loss and restrictions on redemption, creating liquidity risk during periods of market stress.
findings.matters: Concentration of non-liquid assets reduces financial flexibility precisely when the council is entering a phase of high capital spending and declining cash reserves.
findings.figures: Property funds: £17.807m as at 14 Jan 2026 (10.73% of total investments of £165.943m)
findings.quote: However, the value of such investments may fall as well as rise. There may also be restrictions on redemption of the investment. This type of investment is regarded as a 5-to-7-year minimum timeframe.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting implementation will materially affect debt indicators and operational limits, but impact is not yet quantified
findings.detail: Adoption of IFRS 16 from April 2024 will bring lease liabilities onto the balance sheet. The council states it cannot yet estimate the impact on Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit for External Debt because 'the data isn't yet available'. Changes will be reported when data becomes available.
findings.matters: Unquantified changes to key prudential indicators represent reporting uncertainty and potential changes to legal borrowing limits, which could affect the council's ability to deliver the capital programme.
findings.figures: N/A — impact unknown
