findings.quote: At this point the data isn't yet available to make an estimate on the likely impact. When the data is available changes will be made to these two indicators and reported if significant.

findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer departed during 2025/26, with CFO responsibilities transferred to Chief Operating Officer
findings.detail: The strategy document notes that the Chief Finance Officer left the organisation during 2025/26, and treasury management and financial leadership responsibilities have been transferred to the Chief Operating Officer. This represents a significant personnel change during a period of accelerating borrowing and capital investment.
findings.matters: CFO transition poses continuity and capability risk, particularly during period of record debt growth and complex treasury operations. CFO departure may also signal internal challenges.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Following the departure of the Chief Finance Officer in 2025/26, we have changed the references from that post to the Chief Operating Officer.

findings.headline: Treasury strategy depends on interest rates falling from 3.75% to 3.25%, with council using reserves instead of borrowing now to benefit from expected falls
findings.detail: Council is maintaining an under-borrowed position of £2.593m, meaning it is using reserves and cash balances rather than borrowing now. This is described as prudent pending forecast interest rate falls from 3.75% in January 2026 to 3.25% by March 2027. If rates do not fall as forecast, the council will face higher borrowing costs and depleted reserves.
findings.matters: The council's treasury success is betting on a specific market outcome that is outside its control. Forecast error would leave it with both higher costs and lower cash reserves.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing: £2.593m. Current PWLB rates (22 Dec 2025): 5-year 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%. Forecast end Q4 2027: 5-year 4.10%, 10-year 4.70%.
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels during 2026/27 from 3.75% in January 2026 to 3.25% by March 2027.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 58% from £588m to £929m over four years, driven by £142m borrowing requirement on £230m capital programme
findings.detail: The council's total CFR will increase from £588.3m (2024/25 actual) to £929.1m (2028/29 estimate). A capital programme of £229.8m over four years will be financed 62% through borrowing (£142.3m), with the remainder from grants (£51.9m), developer contributions (£5.5m), capital receipts and revenue. External borrowing is forecast to increase by £111m in 2025/26, £126m in 2026/27, £66m in 2027/28, and £29m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Material acceleration in debt burden directly impacts credit profile, interest costs, and future financial flexibility. The 58% four-year growth is substantial.
findings.figures: CFR 2024/25: £588.3m; 2028/29: £929.1m. Total borrowing forecast: £111m, £126m, £66m, £29m in successive years. Capital programme total: £229.778m of which £142.328m borrowing.
findings.quote: It is envisaged, subject to revisions in the capital programme, that external borrowing will increase by £111m over the course of 2025/26, £126m in 2026/27, £66m in 2027/28 and £29m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Macro-economic factors pose very likely and major impact risk to capital programme viability
findings.detail: The capital strategy identifies inflation, interest rates and supply chain issues as risking 'cost, timing and ultimately the viability of the Capital Programme', rated A-II (Very Likely, Major). Mitigation relies on viewing the strategy alongside Treasury Strategy and Revenue Budget documents.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know what external shocks could render capital schemes unviable or force rescoping; interest rate and inflation exposure directly affects the cost of borrowing-funded capital
findings.figures: None specific in covering report
findings.quote: Macro-economic factors, including inflation, interest rates and supply chain issues could impact cost, timing and ultimately the viability of the Capital Programme

findings.headline: Capital funding identified as insufficient to fund investment required for strategic objectives, rated very likely and major impact
findings.detail: The capital strategy risk assessment formally identifies capital funding insufficiency as a risk with A-II rating (Very Likely, Major Impact). The council acknowledges this through reliance on making 'reasonable assumptions' about future financing, reflecting stated uncertainty about availability of grants and other capital finance sources.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's capital programme ambitions are fully funded and deliverable; resource constraints directly affect execution risk and borrowing requirements
findings.figures: Capital programme 'in excess of £230million'
findings.quote: Capital funding is insufficient to fund the investment required to deliver the Council's strategic objectives

findings.headline: Limited assurance that service-level risk registers are in place across the council
findings.detail: The audit opinion notes that only limited assurance can be provided that all services have appropriate risk registers in place, suggesting inconsistent risk management across directorates.
findings.matters: Incomplete risk registers mean service-level risks may not be feeding into the corporate risk register, creating blind spots in the council's overall risk picture.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: only limited assurance can be provided that services have appropriate risk registers in place

findings.headline: One-fifth of internal audit recommendations not yet implemented by the deadline
findings.detail: The audit team's follow-up process found that 12% of actions that were due to be completed in 2024-25 had not been implemented (11 of 92 actions), indicating delays in management remediation of audit findings.
findings.matters: Unimplemented audit recommendations mean known control weaknesses remain unremedied, extending the period during which the council operates with identified governance gaps.
findings.figures: 81 of 92 due actions completed (88%); 11 actions not completed
findings.quote: This follow up process identified that 88% of all actions due to be implemented in 2024-25 (81 of 92 actions) have been completed.

findings.headline: Four internal control reviews rated Red, indicating weak control processes
findings.detail: Out of the 12 finalised internal audit reviews, four resulted in Red ratings, meaning the control process was identified as weak in those areas. While management accepted responsibility for improvement actions, these represent documented control failures.
findings.matters: Red-rated controls mean specific areas of council operation are not adequately protected against risk; this signals control failures that management has yet to remediate.
findings.figures: 4 Red-rated reviews out of 12 finalised reviews; 8 reviews resulted in Amber or Green (more adequate) opinions
findings.quote: four reviews resulted in Red opinions indicating that the control process was weak

findings.headline: Internal audit scope restricted by resourcing constraints
findings.detail: The audit team's work programme was limited by resource impacts, preventing them from examining all risks and completing their planned volume of work. This means gaps in audit coverage exist across the council.
findings.matters: Constrained audit capacity means emerging control weaknesses may not be detected; this is particularly significant given the council already downgraded to limited assurance.
findings.figures: Fieldwork was completed on 19 assurance reviews in 2024-25, with only 3 finalised by year end (9 more from prior year finalised in 2024-25)
findings.quote: The evidence used to draw a reasonable conclusion as to the adequacy and effectiveness of the organisation's risk management, internal control, and governance processes, is however based upon a limited scope due to impacts on resourcing limiting the volume of work that the team have been able to complete

findings.headline: Internal audit downgraded to limited assurance on governance and control framework
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit & Counter Fraud provided an opinion of only limited assurance (not substantial) on the council's governance, risk management, and internal control framework for 2024-25. This is weaker than the typical assurance level and indicates control weaknesses were identified during testing.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on internal audit opinion to assess whether a council's financial controls are effective; limited assurance signals heightened governance risk and weaknesses in how the council manages its money.
findings.figures: Four internal audit reviews out of 12 finalised resulted in Red opinions (weak controls); 88% of agreed audit actions (81 of 92) were completed by the deadline
findings.quote: It is my opinion that only limited assurance can be provided that Medway Council's framework of governance, risk management, and system of internal control, during the year ended 31 March 2025, contributed to the proper, economic, efficient, and effective use of resources in achieving the council's objectives.

findings.headline: Macmillan financial welfare support funding ends June 2026 with £365,000 pressure if not replaced
findings.detail: The council delivers specialist financial welfare support for cancer patients in partnership with Macmillan. Medway expanded from local to regional coverage (North and West Kent) in 2024 at Macmillan's request. However, Macmillan is consulting on the future of directly funded services, and Medway's funding is not confirmed beyond June 2026. If the national scheme ends, this creates a £365,000 pressure from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: External funding that is not renewed forces the council to absorb costs or withdraw services; this is a minor item but illustrates the risk of partnership funding arrangements where the partner organisation changes priorities.
findings.figures: £365,000 pressure if scheme ends
findings.quote: Having delivered specialist financial welfare support for Medway residents with a cancer diagnosis in partnership with Macmillan for many years, in 2024 at Macmillan's request the Council expanded to serve North and West Kent residents. Macmillan are currently consulting on the future of directly funded services and Medway's funding is not confirmed beyond June 2026, so would add a pressure of £365,000 if the national scheme ends.

findings.headline: Council is investing in new care home at Innovation Park (£44 million) while unable to balance base budget
findings.detail: On 29 July 2025, Cabinet agreed to add approximately £44 million to the capital programme for development of a Medway Council owned and operated care home at Innovation Park Medway South. Significant expenditure is not anticipated until late 2026, so 2026/27 impact is expected to be minimal. This is being approved while the council faces a £29.9 million base budget deficit.
findings.matters: A decision to add £44 million to capital investment while the council has a £30 million budget deficit, relies on government emergency support, and holds minimal reserves raises questions about strategic prioritisation and financial governance. The venture into operating a council-owned care home is operationally risky if financial control is not demonstrated elsewhere.
findings.figures: £44 million capital addition approved; expenditure expected late 2026 onwards
findings.quote: On 29 July the Cabinet agreed to recommend to Council the addition of a total of c£44million to the Council's capital programme for the development of a Medway Council owned and operated care home at Innovation Park Medway (IPM) South.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care demographic growth of 50 additional placements per year creates uncontrollable cost growth
findings.detail: Children's Social Care projections assume demographic growth of 50 additional placements each year over the medium term, adding £1.199 million in 2026/27 alone. Placement cost uplifts are projected at 3.6% for 2026/27. The council is also investing £234,000 to recruit more internal foster carers, suggesting insufficient in-house capacity to meet demand at current cost.
findings.matters: If placement demand growth is structural (50 per year every year), this is an open-ended commitment with no cost control mechanism; the council will be forced to continue spending to meet statutory duties.
findings.figures: 50 additional placements per year; £1.199 million cost in 2026/27; 3.6% placement cost uplift
findings.quote: As with Adult Social Care and as in previous years, this pressure is primarily driven by demographic growth estimated at a further 50 placements each year over the medium term compared to the current budget, adding £1.199million in 2026/27.

findings.headline: 64% of £229.6 million capital programme is funded through borrowing at high interest rates, adding treasury cost risk
findings.detail: The council's capital programme stands at £229.606 million with 64% funded through borrowing. High interest rates continue to impact the financing cost of capital. The interest and financing budget also funds Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) for debt repayment. If the council were to borrow the full projected 2026/27 deficit of £29.942 million through EFS, this would require "a further growth in the Interest & Financing budget of c£1million" just for that year.
findings.matters: High borrowing at elevated interest rates locks in elevated treasury costs; additional borrowing to fund ongoing deficits compounds the problem. Lenders need assurance that capital investment is constrained and that the council is not relying on ever-larger borrowing to fund revenue services.
findings.figures: £229.606 million capital programme; 64% funded through borrowing; c£1 million additional annual treasury cost for each £29.942 million EFS
findings.quote: Around 64% of the Council's current capital programme of £229.606million is funded through borrowing and high interest rates continue to impact the financing of the capital programme.

findings.headline: Funding uncertainty from Fair Funding Review 2.0 could materially alter council income with no transitional protection confirmed
findings.detail: The government is consulting on the Fair Funding Review 2.0, which will shift funding distribution based on an updated needs assessment. Medway's high deprivation ranking could see "materially significant gains" but the council's funding advisors project that "there is no funding in the settlement for transitional arrangements." Pessimistic and optimistic scenarios show income variance of £19.8 million (£21.2 million vs £41.1 million growth vs 2025/26 budget). The MTFO retains February 2025 projections "as reflecting our best estimate at this stage" but notes uncertainty.
findings.matters: A £20 million swing in future income depending on funding reform implementation creates material forecast uncertainty; if transitional protection is limited, Medway could face sudden cliff-edge funding cuts or gains that destabilise medium-term planning.
findings.figures: Optimistic scenario: £41.083 million growth; base case: £33.279 million growth; pessimistic scenario: £21.240 million growth (all vs 2025/26 budget)
findings.quote: Based on the proposals in the latest phase of the funding reforms consultation, Medway's relatively high Indices of Multiple Deprivation rank would result in us receiving a greater share of national allocations. Our funding advisors are currently projecting that the new methodology would see materially significant gains in the national share of funding allocated to Medway in future, however there is no funding in the settlement for transitional arrangements.

findings.headline: Council has received £20.239 million Exceptional Financial Support in 2024/25 and expects to need further support for 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council received £18.484 million through a capitalisation direction to balance the 2025/26 budget. For 2024/25, the government agreed in principle to an expanded EFS request taking total support to £20.239 million (within the agreed amount of £23.171 million). The MTFO states: "This MTFO therefore suggests that it will again be necessary for the Council to see support from the government through the Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) scheme." To fund the 2026/27 gap alone would require an additional £29.942 million EFS.
findings.matters: Dependence on government capitalisation directions to balance budgets is not sustainable; if EFS is withdrawn or constrained, the council will face a Section 114 notice and financial crisis. The Council is effectively insolvent without government support.
findings.figures: £18.484 million capitalisation direction 2025/26; £20.239 million total EFS 2024/25; £29.942 million would be required for 2026/27 gap alone
findings.quote: This MTFO therefore suggests that it will again be necessary for the Council to see support from the government through the Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) scheme. At this stage, in order to fund the budget gap projected in this MTFO, it would be necessary to request an additional £29.942million EFS for 2026/27.

findings.headline: SEND statutory assessment requests have doubled, requiring £1.6 million investment to meet statutory timeframes
findings.detail: The Education directorate is facing a doubling of requests for special educational needs assessments. To meet statutory assessment timeframes, the council must invest £1.6 million in additional staffing in 2026/27. This is a new statutory obligation that cannot be deferred or reduced without legal risk.
findings.matters: A doubling of statutory SEND assessments represents uncontrollable demand growth; the council cannot refuse to assess or meet legal timescales. This creates an unfunded mandate that will recur and likely grow.
findings.figures: £1.6 million investment required for 2026/27; doubling of needs assessment requests noted
findings.quote: Due to the doubling of requests for needs assessments, it is necessary to invest in additional staffing in order to meet statutory SEND assessment timeframes, projected to cost £1.600million.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care costs increasing by £18.954 million in 2026/27 driven by service pressure, not demand alone
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is projected to grow by £18.954 million in 2026/27. The primary driver is £7.596 million for cost of current service pressure (placements exceeding current budget), £6.504 million for price uplifts (5% per annum) toward fair cost of care, £3.137 million for 3% demographic growth, and £3.365 million to realign staffing budgets. The council is legally obliged to provide care for all eligible individuals regardless of ability to pay.
findings.matters: A £7.6 million overspend on placements beyond budget suggests the council's cost control has slipped and the baseline is understated; combined with demographic growth and statutory obligation to provide care, this creates an open-ended commitment that is difficult to manage or control.
findings.figures: £18.954 million total increase; £7.596 million current service pressure; £6.504 million price uplift; £3.137 million demographic growth (3%); £3.365 million staffing realignment
findings.quote: The primary drivers are the cost of placements in excess of the current year budget (referred to as the cost of current service pressure) of £7.596million and uplifts of £6.504million (broadly 5% a year across the medium term) to progress towards the fair cost of care and to reflect inflation and support the increased national minimum wage pay to carers by providers. The Council is legally obliged to provide care for all eligible individuals regardless of payment status.

findings.headline: General Reserves at less than 2% of budget with overspend already exceeding reserves in 2025/26
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, General Reserves are projected at £10.011 million, representing less than 2% of the 2025/26 net revenue budget of £500.659 million. The first round budget monitoring for 2025/26 already projects an overspend of £10.948 million, which exceeds the General Reserve balance of £10.061 million. The Section 151 Officer has set an aspiration to grow reserves to 5% of net budget (approximately £25 million).
findings.matters: Reserves below 2% leave the council with minimal buffer for financial shocks; an overspend already exceeding reserves in the current year means the council has no safety net and will need to draw down earmarked reserves or request emergency government support.
findings.figures: General Reserves £10.011 million, 2025/26 overspend £10.948 million, General Reserve balance £10.061 million, target 5% of budget circa £25 million
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council is projected to hold £10.011million in general reserves. The General Reserves balance therefore represents less than 2% of the 2025/26 net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Budget deficit of £29.942 million for 2026/27 with no funding solution identified yet
findings.detail: The Council faces a projected budget gap of £29.942 million for 2026/27, rising to £191.257 million cumulatively over the medium term. The Cabinet has instructed directorates to identify savings and income generation proposals, but the MTFO acknowledges that "after successive years of making savings and increasing efficiency, it is becoming ever more difficult to reduce costs without materially impacting on service delivery." No mitigating proposals are currently included in the projection.
findings.matters: A council unable to identify a funding solution for its projected deficit is a material credit risk; lenders need confidence in the council's capacity to balance its budget or obtain sustainable government support.
findings.figures: £29.942 million (2026/27 gap), £191.257 million (cumulative medium-term gap)
findings.quote: The Cabinet notes the projected budget requirement, the Council's resource assumptions, and the resultant projected budget shortfall for 2026/27 of £29.942million and a cumulative £191.257million shortfall over the medium term.

findings.headline: Interest and financing budget assumes no additional cost for the £29.942m EFS borrowing that would be required to fund 2026/27 gap, masking true deficit scale
findings.detail: Section 10.3.3 notes that if the Council needs to borrow an additional £29.942m for EFS in 2026/27, it would require 'further growth in the Interest & Financing budget of c£1million to fund the borrowing required'. However, this MTFO 'does not include any addition to the budget to cover this treasury cost at this stage'. This means the projections show the 'raw' gap without the cost of financing it — the real gap is at least £1m larger if EFS is drawn.
findings.matters: The gap is artificially small because it excludes the financing cost of bridging it. The true structural deficit is larger than stated, and the debt will persist beyond the medium term.
findings.figures: £29.942m EFS required; c£1m additional interest cost not budgeted
findings.quote: it would be necessary to request an additional £29.942million EFS for 2026/27. This would require a further growth in the Interest & Financing budget of c£1million to fund the borrowing required, however as officers and Members continue to work to reduce this potential gap, this MTFO does not include any addition to the budget to cover this treasury cost at this stage.

findings.headline: Funding reform (Fair Funding Review 2.0) creates uncertain upside but no downside protection, and settlement for 2026/27 will not be known until November/December
findings.detail: The Government has consulted on fair funding reforms that could shift distribution towards deprivation-based need. Medway's high Indices of Multiple Deprivation rank suggests it would gain significantly under the new methodology. However, the funding advisors project Medway will receive 'significantly less than the new methodology calculates' in 2026/27, with gains phasing in only gradually to 2028/29 — because authorities losing funding will be protected through slower increases for gainers. No clarity is expected until the Provisional Settlement in November/December. The Council is therefore planning on February 2025 assumptions with high uncertainty.
findings.matters: Material funding uncertainty in a council already in structural deficit creates planning risk. Lenders assess funding volatility as a proxy for revenue stability.
findings.figures: Base projections hold February 2025 assumptions; optimistic scenario £41.083m growth; pessimistic scenario £21.240m growth
findings.quote: it is not possible to determine with any confidence the future funding streams the Council can expect... our assumption is that Medway will receive significantly less than the new methodology calculates we should in 2026/27, gradually increasing to the 'correct' level by the end of this SR period.

findings.headline: £44m care home capital project approved on 29 July with no treasury cost reflected in this MTFO, meaning interest costs will worsen 2026/27 projections
findings.detail: Cabinet agreed on 29 July to add c£44m to the capital programme for an owned and operated care home at Innovation Park Medway South. The Council notes it does not expect significant expenditure until late 2026, so treasury costs are 'expected to be minimal' for 2026/27. However, this glosses over future-year borrowing costs that are not yet budgeted and will worsen the medium-term position. Borrowing 64% of the current £229.6m capital programme at high interest rates already creates financing pressure.
findings.matters: A major capital commitment not yet reflected in treasury budgets represents a hidden liability. At 64% loan-funded and with high interest rates, this will add material MRP and interest costs in future years, worsening the structural deficit.
findings.figures: c£44m capital approval; 64% of current £229.606m programme funded via borrowing
findings.quote: On 29 July the Cabinet agreed to recommend to Council the addition of a total of c£44million to the Council's capital programme for the development of a Medway Council owned and operated care home at Innovation Park Medway (IPM) South... it is not anticipated that significant expenditure will be made until late 2026 and the impact on the treasury budgets for 2026/27 is therefore expected to be minimal.

findings.headline: Capitalisation direction for 2024/25 (£20.239m) has been agreed 'in principle' but risk of non-grant if conditions breached creates Section 114 Notice risk
findings.detail: The Council's 2024/25 budget was balanced on the basis of a 'minded to' decision from the Minister for Exceptional Financial Support (capitalisation direction), subject to conditions. Section 15 (Risk Management) flags that if EFS is not actually granted, the Council would not have a balanced budget and the Section 151 Officer would be required to issue a Section 114 notice. This is a severe governance event that signals insolvency and can trigger administration procedures.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration of inability to set a balanced budget and triggers legal intervention. Lenders view this as a credit event equivalent to default.
findings.figures: £20.239m 2024/25 EFS at risk; £18.484m 2025/26 capitalisation direction at risk
findings.quote: There is therefore a risk that the EFS/capitalisation direction may not be granted, meaning the Council's budget for the current year would not be balanced, meaning the Section 151 Officer would be required to issue a Section 114 Notice.

findings.headline: Calculation error in February 2025 projections revealed mid-year (£1.484m expenditure omitted), indicating control weaknesses in financial planning
findings.detail: When the Council set its 2025/26 budget in February 2025, it calculated a budget gap of £10.070m. However, an error in that calculation omitted £1.484m of expenditure, meaning the true gap should have been £11.554m. This error was only discovered during preparation of this MTFO. The error suggests weaknesses in the financial planning control environment.
findings.matters: A material calculation error in budget setting six months ago, only discovered now, raises questions about the robustness of the Council's financial planning and reporting. Lenders rely on the accuracy of council disclosures.
findings.figures: £1.484m omitted from February 2025 gap calculation
findings.quote: an error in the calculation omitted £1.484million of expenditure from that gap, which should have been £11.554million

findings.headline: SEND transport demand rising c£1.2m per year across the medium term, after investment to reduce placements by only 5% has had limited effect
findings.detail: Education is projecting growing SEND transport costs of c£1.2m per year across the medium term. Even after targeting a 5% reduction in pupils with EHCPs receiving SEND transport (a major intervention), the 2026/27 increase is still £1.528m for SEND transport alone. This indicates demographic/need growth outpacing mitigation efforts.
findings.matters: SEND pressure is structural and statutory — councils must provide transport for children with education health and care plans. Rising demand beyond savings efforts suggests demographic headwinds that will persist across the sector.
findings.figures: c£1.2m additional SEND transport per year; 2026/27 SEND transport pressure of £1.528m despite targeting 5% reduction in placements
findings.quote: the proportion of pupils with EHCPs receiving SEND transport is targeted to reduce by 5%, with both these mitigations the increase in transport costs has been reduced to £1.528million for SEND transport... The MTFO includes projected growth across the medium term for SEND transport adding c£1.2million a year

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs rising £1m in 2026/27 and a further £500k in 2027/28, unmitigated
findings.detail: Culture and Community services face a £1m pressure in 2026/27 driven by the continued high cost of temporary accommodation for homeless households, with a further £500k cost projected in 2027/28. The Council provides this as a statutory obligation but has not identified offsetting savings or income to cover it.
findings.matters: Growing homelessness costs signal housing market failure and rising social vulnerability in the area. This is a statutory cost councils cannot control and suggests deteriorating community conditions.
findings.quote: The continued level of demand and high cost of providing temporary accommodation for homeless households is the primary driver at a pressure of £1.000million, with a further £500,000 cost projected in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care costs rising £18.954m in 2026/27 alone, driven by placement costs and demographic growth neither contained nor funded
findings.detail: Adult Social Care expenditure is projected to increase £18.954m in 2026/27. Key drivers are £7.596m from current service placement pressure (overspend against budget), £6.504m from care cost uplifts towards the Fair Cost of Care, and £3.137m from 3% demographic growth. The Council is legally obliged to provide care for all eligible individuals regardless of payment status, so these costs cannot be cut without breaching statutory duty.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable statutory social care costs that outpace funding increases are a sign of structural insolvency risk. Lenders use social care pressure as a leading indicator of council distress.
findings.figures: £18.954m increase 2026/27; £7.596m current service pressure; £6.504m uplifts; £3.137m demographic growth (3% pa)
findings.quote: Adult Social Care costs are projected to increase by a net £18.954 million in 2026/27. The primary drivers are the cost of placements in excess of the current year budget (referred to as the cost of current service pressure) of £7.596million and uplifts of £6.504million (broadly 5% a year across the medium term)

findings.headline: General reserves depleted to 1.9% of budget, far below the 5% minimum aspired to by the Section 151 Officer
findings.detail: The Council is projected to hold £10.011m in general reserves at 31 March 2026, representing less than 2% of the £500.7m net revenue budget. The Section 151 Officer's aspiration is 5% (c£25m) to provide financial resilience against shocks. The Council is operating with minimal buffer, and a single unplanned pressure could trigger a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: Reserves below 2% of budget leave no buffer for demand shocks, income shortfalls, or emergency costs. This signals poor financial resilience and increases default risk.
findings.figures: £10.011m reserves = 1.9% of £500.659m budget; aspiration is 5% = c£25.000m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council is projected to hold £10.011million in general reserves. The General Reserves balance therefore represents less than 2% of the 2025/26 net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £29.9m for 2026/27 rising to £191.3m cumulatively, requiring government Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Even after three years of Exceptional Financial Support (£20.2m in 2024/25, £18.5m in 2025/26), the Council faces a £29.9m gap in 2026/27 and £191.3m total across five years. The Council projects it will again require EFS, this time £29.9m for 2026/27 alone. Without government support or major service cuts, the budget cannot be balanced.
findings.matters: Serial reliance on exceptional government funding indicates structural revenue insufficiency. Lenders view repeated bailouts as indicating unsustainable service/cost structures and reduced repayment capacity for debt service.
findings.figures: £29.942m gap 2026/27; £191.257m cumulative gap; three consecutive years of EFS (2024/25 £20.239m, 2025/26 £18.484m, 2026/27 £29.942m requested)
findings.quote: This MTFO therefore suggests that it will again be necessary for the Council to see support from the government through the Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) scheme.

findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) already overspending by £10.948m, exceeding the entire general reserve of £10.061m
findings.detail: The Council's first budget monitoring round for 2025/26 projects an overspend of £10.948m, which exceeds the general reserve balance. The Section 151 Officer will need to identify material expenditure reductions in-year to avoid the overspend consuming and depleting the reserves entirely. This is a working capital crisis.
findings.matters: A council overspending beyond its reserves in the current year signals immediate financial distress and triggers governance interventions. Lenders assess working capital health as a proxy for credit risk.
findings.figures: £10.948m overspend against £10.061m general reserves
findings.quote: projected an overspend of £10.948million, a figure in excess of the general reserve balance at 31 March 2025 of £10.061million

news_drafts.headline: Void times for temporary accommodation are long enough that the council prioritises a dedicated repairs contract to reduce them
news_drafts.lead: Extended voids directly reduce rental income from temporary accommodation and undermine the efficiency of the council's emergency housing provision, affecting financial sustainability of the HRA.

news_drafts.headline: Repairs and maintenance work for council housing is currently outside the scope of the existing HRA contract, creating performance risk
news_drafts.lead: The HRA is ring-fenced for financial purposes; disruption to contractor performance directly threatens the council's ability to maintain service delivery, asset management, and rental income across its housing stock.

news_drafts.headline: Council is relying on predominantly short-term borrowing due to market volatility, facing £150m refinancing need in the year ahead
news_drafts.lead: Heavy reliance on short-term borrowing and refinancing of £150m during elevated rates creates significant refinancing risk and makes the council vulnerable to further rate rises or market disruption.
